title: Ming China and the Closed Door

cards.h: The empire that shut its doors
cards.b:
The Ming dynasty ruled China from 1368 to 1644. It built the Forbidden City, sent huge fleets across the Indian Ocean and made blue-and-white porcelain famous. Then, from the 1500s on, it limited sea trade.

Why did a rich, sea-going empire pull back? Historians still argue about the answer. The story matters because it shapes how we see China and the world.

Zhu Yuanzhang, once a poor peasant and a Buddhist monk, led the rebels who drove out the Mongol Yuan dynasty. He founded the Ming in 1368 and took the name Hongwu. He restored the civil service exams and ordered new land surveys.

Hongwu was suspicious of his own officials and ruled with harsh punishments. His early policies set patterns of control that his successors kept.

Yongle, Hongwu's son, seized the throne in 1402. He moved the capital north to Beijing and began the Forbidden City in 1406, which was finished around 1420. He also repaired the Grand Canal and sent out the great naval voyages of Zheng He.

The Forbidden City has more than 900 buildings, and it was the seat of power for Ming and later Qing emperors. It shows how the Ming wanted to project order and centrality.

Ray Huang, 1587, A Year of No Significance (1981)

Huang chose one ordinary year, 1587, and showed how the Ming state worked from the inside. The emperor stayed away from court, and officials argued over rules, money and power.

The book shows that the state had a rigid system, and that small disputes could block big decisions. It helps explain the later caution about the sea.
The timeline shows how the state's sea power grew, then pulled back, and then collapsed under rebellion and invasion.

Blue-and-white porcelain was one of the great Chinese exports, sold across the Islamic world and Europe. In exchange, China took in silver from Japan in the 1500s and from the Americas by the 1570s. Spanish galleons from Manila brought Mexican silver to Asia.

Silver became the currency of trade. It was also needed for taxes, and the Ming state came to depend on it. That dependency made the empire sensitive to shifts in the silver supply.

A popular image shows the Ming as isolated, uninterested in the outside world, and closed by a single decree. The phrase "closed door" is used for that picture.

Historians argue the reality was messy. Private overseas trade was banned for long periods, but goods still moved through Portuguese ports, Japanese traders and smugglers. The "closed door" was partial and changed over time.

From the 1300s onward the Ming banned private overseas trade several times. The aim was to stop pirates, called wokou, who raided the coasts. The ban also helped the state keep control over trade through official tribute missions.

Smugglers ignored the bans, and coastal families grew rich on illegal trade. The gap between the law and the market created tensions that grew with time.

In the 1580s the minister Zhang Juzheng pushed a reform called the single whip. It combined many taxes into one payment, made mainly in silver. It was meant to simplify the system and to cut corruption.

The reform made silver central to government, and it tied the empire's finances to global silver flows. When silver supply shifted, the Ming felt it deeply.

Zheng He made seven voyages between 1405 and 1433. Historians argue the reasons for stopping them. Some point to cost and to the rise of Confucian officials who distrusted eunuch admirals. Others point to the threat from the Mongol frontier.

The question is not only about China. It shows how far a rich state can turn its back on the sea, and how a choice can shape centuries.

Zheng He's fleets reached the Indian coast. They visited Calicut and Cochin in the early 1400s, and in 1411 they fought the king of Ceylon and took him to China as a prisoner.

Calicut was a great pepper port, and Chinese silk and porcelain reached its markets. The Indian Ocean was a busy network of kingdoms, and Ming ships were only one part of it.

Five things to remember
  1. The Ming ruled from 1368 to 1644.
  2. Yongle moved the capital to Beijing and built the Forbidden City.
  3. Zheng He sailed from 1405 to 1433.
  4. Silver reached China from Japan and the Americas.
  5. The single whip reform tied taxes to silver.
Think about it
  • Was the closed door a choice or a set of responses to problems?
  • How did silver change the power of a state?
